hints.junior: Short cache lifetimes feel safe, but they mean everyone re-downloads the same unchanged file over and over. That's the opposite of what caching is for.
hints.mid: Same-named asset + short Cache-Control is a tradeoff you don't have to make once hashing enters the picture.
hints.staff: The real bug here is that HTML and its hashed assets need opposite caching policies, one mutable pointer, one immutable payload.

hints.junior: Toggle between the two modes and watch which requests actually hit the network on the second and third simulated visit.
hints.mid: The fixed mode's request log should go quiet after the first load until the hash itself changes.
hints.staff: The broken mode's 'stale after deploy' state is a 200 from cache, not an error, that's exactly why it's hard to catch in monitoring.

hints.junior: The filename itself becomes the cache key. Change the file, change the name, and the old cached copy just stops being requested.
hints.mid: max-age=31536000 plus immutable only makes sense once the URL is a pure function of the content.
hints.staff: This turns cache invalidation, notoriously hard, into a non-problem: there's nothing to invalidate, only a new URL to start requesting.

hints.junior: The HTML file is the one exception, it always needs a short cache lifetime so the browser can learn the new hashed filenames.
hints.mid: no-cache on the HTML entry point forces a cheap revalidation (a 304) on every load instead of skipping the request entirely.
hints.staff: A service worker's cache lifecycle doesn't inherit HTTP Cache-Control for free, if one exists, it needs this same discipline applied on purpose.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about a static file that never changes name between deploys, so browsers end up re-downloading it constantly, or worse, serving a stale copy after you ship a fix.
sections.mid: A same-named asset with a short or default cache lifetime forces a permanent tradeoff — cache too long and a real deploy goes unnoticed, cache too short and you're re-serving the same bytes for nothing.
sections.staff: Content-hashed filenames dissolve the tradeoff entirely — cache lifetime and correctness become independent variables instead of one knob you have to compromise on.

sections.junior: The fix is to bake a content hash into the filename, so the URL itself changes the moment the file does, and cache that URL forever with no risk.
sections.mid: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on a content-hashed asset is safe specifically because the URL is a function of the content — the HTML that references it is what actually changes on deploy.
sections.staff: The HTML document and its hashed assets need opposite caching policies — the HTML is the mutable pointer revalidated on every request, while everything it points to is immutable and cached for a year.

sections.junior: Try the short-lived cache mode first, then switch to hashed and immutable, and watch how many requests actually go out on the repeat visits.
sections.mid: The fixed mode caches the hashed URL for the full session and only re-fetches once the hash itself changes.
sections.staff: The broken mode is stale for the entire cache window even after a real deploy — not just slow, actually wrong content served with a 200 from cache.

sections.junior: Hash your asset filenames, cache them forever, and keep the HTML that points to them on a short lifetime so it always finds the latest hash.
sections.mid: Cache hashed assets forever with immutable, and keep the HTML that references them on a short or no-cache lifetime so it always picks up the new hash.
sections.staff: A service worker's own cache lifecycle doesn't inherit HTTP Cache-Control semantics — apply the same short-pointer, long-payload discipline to it deliberately.
